intuition: A sorted list exposes its smallest remaining element at its head. Instead of collecting values and sorting them again, compare the two heads and repeatedly select the smaller one. This is the same merge operation used by merge sort, except that the output is built by reconnecting existing nodes.

The output tail marks the last node already chosen. A dummy node gives that tail an initial home before any real node has been selected, avoiding a separate first-node branch. After attaching a node, advance the pointer for the input it came from and then advance the output tail.

When one input becomes empty, the other suffix needs no more comparisons. It is already sorted, and every value in it is at least the last selected value. Splicing this suffix onto the tail finishes the merge without allocating replacement nodes. Equal values may come from either input; both original nodes still have to appear.

steps: Begin with list1=1→2→4 and list2=1→3→4, with tail pointing to the dummy.
The two heads tie at 1. Select list1’s first node, leaving its next head at 2.
Compare 2 with list2’s 1; select that second 1. Next select 2 before 3.
Select 3, then select list1’s 4 when the two remaining heads tie.
List1 is now exhausted. Attach list2’s final 4 and return dummy.next, yielding 1→1→2→3→4→4.

codeNotes.note: The dummy is an output anchor, not a value included in the answer. It makes empty-input cases follow the same control flow.
Relinking preserves the selected input node rather than copying its value into a replacement node.
The remaining suffix is already ordered, so a single link completes all remaining work.
